rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own column experiment (25 L soil N uptake monitoring columns, Candler fine sand, two seasons, four replicates) in which KNO3 was applied 1, 3 or 7 d before a weekly forced leaching event; measured plant N uptake, biomass, ear yield, root length density and FUE (Table 1, Fig. 4-6).
rows.notes: The study does not test soil sensors, irrigation scheduling or frequent small-volume irrigation. It artificially manipulates fertilizer residence time by forcing a leaching event with 2 pore volumes of water at fixed intervals and treats longer residence time only as 'indicative of' better irrigation practices. Columns were kept near field capacity throughout, so crop water stress was not studied. Its own result is that longer N residence time increased growth, ear yield, N uptake and FUE (Table 1); any link to sensor-based scheduling is inferred by the authors, not measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own column experiment with three N residence-time treatments over two seasons; potential N leaching calculated as weekly applied N minus measured plant uptake (Fig. 7).
rows.notes: No soil sensor or irrigation scheduling treatment was tested; residence time was imposed by forced weekly leaching of the columns with ~2 pore volumes. 'Potential N leaching' is a calculated difference (applied N minus plant uptake) rather than measured leaching under a scheduled irrigation regime. The study's own result is that longer fertilizer residence time reduced calculated potential N leaching (253/223/101 kg N ha-1 fall; 282/159/85 spring for 1, 3, 7 d), which the authors interpret as indicative of improved irrigation management, but the claimed technology (sensor-based frequent small-volume irrigation) was not evaluated.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a controlled column experiment on nitrogen residence time in sweet corn, cited by the review as support for irrigation scheduling/sensor-based irrigation; the connection is interpretive, not experimental.
